transcript.text: The sides of our new fridge freezer get really warm, almost hot, especially near the front edge. Is that a fire risk? It's in an alcove between two units.

In almost all cases this is normal and not a fire risk. Most modern fridge freezers don't have the old black grille on the back. Instead, the pipes that get rid of the heat taken out of the food run just under the side panels. There's also a warm pipe around the front edge of the cabinet. Its job is to stop condensation forming where the door seal touches. That's why the sides, and especially the front edge, can feel very warm, sometimes uncomfortably so. These pipes carry refrigerant, not mains electricity, so the warmth itself isn't a fire hazard. In your case two things could make it warmer than usual. First, being new, it may still be in its first cool-down, when it runs hard for up to 24 hours or so. Second, an alcove between units can trap the heat if the gaps are tight. A few quick checks to tell normal from not-quite-right: 1. Check the installation gaps. Look in the manual for the clearance needed at the sides, top and back. Many models with side condensers need a few centimetres each side and space above for the warm air to rise. If it's squeezed in tighter than that, it will run hotter and work harder. Easing it out a little, or making sure there's an air gap above, often makes a noticeable difference. 2. Check the doors close and seal. Make sure nothing is stopping either door, then run your fingers round the seals for gaps or folds. A door that isn't sealing makes the compressor run almost constantly, and the sides then stay hot. 3. Check it's cooling and cycling. Give it a day with the doors kept shut, then see whether the fridge is cold (about 3–5°C) and the freezer is freezing. Listen to whether it goes quiet for spells. Warm sides plus good cooling plus normal on/off running means it's behaving as designed. The warning signs that would make it a fault are:
• a burning or electrical smell
• heat coming from the back bottom corner (where the compressor and wiring are) rather than the sides
• the adjoining units discolouring or getting hot
• the fridge running constantly without ever reaching temperature If any of those happen, switch it off and contact the retailer or manufacturer. As it's new, it's under warranty, so they should come out to it. It's also worth putting the make and model into the manufacturer's recall checker or the GOV.UK product safety alerts page for peace of mind. To narrow it down: is it keeping food properly cold
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]

Yes, it's keeping everything cold - fridge is at 4C and freezer at -18C. No burning smell either. The gaps are quite tight though, about 1cm each side and a few cm above. I'd rather not pull it out as the floor is new.

That's reassuring. A fridge at 4°C and a freezer at -18°C, with no burning smell, means the cooling system is doing its job. Warm sides on a fridge freezer like this are the heat it's designed to get rid of, so it isn't a fire risk. The tight gaps are the one thing I'd take note of. With only about 1cm each side, the heat from those side pipes has nowhere to go. That's why they feel almost hot rather than just warm. It's not dangerous, but it does make the compressor work harder. That can mean higher running costs and, over years, more wear. Many side-condenser models ask for more space than that, so it's worth checking the manual or the installation sheet for your model's figure. 1. Keep the space above clear. Don't store boxes or trays on top, and make sure there's no cupboard closing off the top of the alcove. Warm air needs to rise out, so this is the easiest gain.
2. Check the front plinth. Some models draw cooling air in at the bottom front, so keep any vent or grille there free of mats or clutter.
3. Watch whether it cycles. Over an hour or so, see if it goes quiet for spells. If it does, the tight fit is costing a little efficiency but nothing more. If it hums almost non-stop, the heat isn't escaping well enough (or a door isn't sealing), and it would be worth acting on.
4. Feel the units either side now and then. Warm is fine. Hot to the touch, or any discolouring or peeling, would mean it needs more space. Slide a piece of hardboard or thick cardboard in front of it first, or use furniture sliders. Even easing it forward a couple of centimetres opens up air at the back and sides. If it runs constantly, or the neighbouring units get hot, contact the retailer or manufacturer while it's under warranty. They can confirm the clearance your model really needs. Otherwise I'd treat it as normal and leave it be. One thing would settle it: over an hour or so, does it go quiet for spells between running, or does it seem to hum almost non-stop?

I haven't watched it for an hour yet. It just has the normal hum as far as I can tell. The manual says to leave space but I didn't check the exact figure, so I'll look. Is 1cm each side definitely okay in the meantime?

For safety, yes. With the fridge at 4°C, the freezer at -18°C and no burning smell, 1cm each side isn't a fire risk in the meantime, and you can carry on using it normally. Those side pipes carry refrigerant, not mains power, so a tight fit doesn't make them dangerous. What I can't promise is that 1cm is fine long term. That depends on the figure in your manual. If it asks for more, the tight fit mainly costs efficiency and adds a bit of wear over the years. It isn't a hazard, and it doesn't need sorting today. In the meantime:
1. Find the clearance figure in the manual. If 1cm meets it, you're done and the warmth is simply normal. If it asks for noticeably more, it's worth easing it out when convenient, with the floor protected as mentioned.
2. Keep the top clear. The few centimetres above are your main escape route for warm air, so don't let anything sit on top or close it in.
3. When you happen to be in the kitchen for a while, notice whether it goes quiet now and then. A normal hum that stops at intervals is fine. One that never stops would suggest the heat isn't getting away well enough. If the units either side ever get hot or discoloured, or you notice a burning smell, switch it off and contact the retailer while it's under warranty. Otherwise this looks like normal behaviour. What side and top clearance does the manual ask for?

I don't know the figure off the top of my head, I only know the manual says to leave space and I haven't checked exactly. I'll look it up. If it asks for more than 1cm, what should I do given I don't want to pull the fridge out because of the new floor?

If the manual asks for more than 1cm, you don't need to haul it right out. A few centimetres forward is usually enough, and that can be done without marking a new floor. Your options, easiest first: 1. Roll it forward a little, not out. Most fridge freezers have rollers at the back and screw-adjustable feet at the front. Wind the front feet up until it rests on its rollers. Lay hardboard, an offcut of vinyl or a doubled sheet of thick card on the floor in front. Then ease it straight forward 2–5cm, with two people, keeping it square so it doesn't twist or drag sideways. Wind the feet back down so it sits level with the doors swinging shut. Coming forward opens the air path round the back and up the sides, which is often most of the benefit.
2. Make the most of the top gap. If there's a cupboard or shelf closing off the top of the alcove, opening that up or keeping it completely clear helps the warm air escape. That alone can make a real difference.
3. Ask the retailer or installer. If they delivered and fitted it, ask them to set it to the manufacturer's clearances. They have the floor protectors and experience. It's also worth asking them whether the tight fit affects your warranty, as some manufacturers expect their installation figures to be followed.
4. Leave it, knowingly. If you'd rather not touch it, it's still not a safety issue. The cost is mainly a bit more electricity and some extra wear on the compressor over the years. If the units either side get hot or discolour, or it seems to run without ever pausing, that would tip the balance towards moving it. Otherwise, warm sides with the fridge at 4°C and freezer at -18°C is the appliance working as designed.
